# **1\. Introduction**

This Software Architecture Document (SAD) provides an overview of the architecture of AudioLIT, an interactive web-based tool that helps people understand how speech-based artificial-intelligence models make their decisions. It presents the system through several architectural views, each describing a different aspect of the design, so that the important design decisions are captured and can be explained and justified.

## **1.1 Purpose**

The purpose of this document is to capture and communicate the significant architectural decisions made for AudioLIT. It serves as the main reference for the development team when building the system, and it allows the project mentor, teaching assistant, and examiners to assess whether the proposed structure is sound and whether it meets the requirements agreed in the Software Requirements Specification (SRS).

The document is written for several audiences. The development team uses it as the agreed plan for how the system fits together before writing code. The mentor and teaching assistant use it to judge whether the design is well thought out and complete. Examiners use it to understand the system quickly and to see where each team member's contribution lies. Future students who might extend the project use it to understand the structure without having to read all of the code. The document therefore aims to be clear and self-contained, explaining not only what the design is but why each significant choice was made.

An important characteristic of AudioLIT is that it is built as an extension of an existing open-source project called ECHO 1.0, rather than being written from scratch. ECHO 1.0 is a speech-model interpretability tool developed within the department in a previous year. Because AudioLIT builds on top of it, this document is careful to explain which parts of the system are inherited from ECHO 1.0, which parts are extended, and which parts are entirely new. This makes the design easier to understand and shows clearly where the new contribution of this project lies.

## **1.2 Scope**

This document applies to the whole of the AudioLIT platform: the web-based user interface, the backend server, the background processing system that runs the AI models, the storage used for caching results and for keeping records, and the model, explanation, and audio-analysis services behind them. Features that are inherited unchanged from ECHO 1.0 are described only where AudioLIT changes or extends them. Some advanced research features are planned but are not part of the committed delivery; these are noted as future work and are designed so they can be added later without changing the core structure.

## **1.3 Definitions, Acronyms, and Abbreviations**

| Term | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| ASR | Automatic Speech Recognition \- converting spoken audio into written text. |
| SER | Speech Emotion Recognition \- identifying the emotion in a person's speech. |
| ADD | Audio Deepfake Detection \- deciding whether speech is genuine or artificially generated, and explaining why. |
| XAI | Explainable Artificial Intelligence \- techniques that make an AI model's decisions understandable to people. |
| ECHO 1.0 | The existing open-source speech-interpretability tool that AudioLIT extends. |
| Attribution / Saliency | A visual explanation showing which parts of the audio most influenced the model's decision. |
| Spectrogram | A visual representation of sound that shows how its frequencies change over time. |
| Whisper / Wav2Vec2 | Well-known families of pre-trained speech models used for transcription and audio understanding. |
| Cache | A store of previously computed results that lets the system return an answer instantly instead of recomputing it. |
| Hugging Face | An online hub from which pre-trained AI models can be downloaded. |

## **1.5 Overview**

The rest of this document is organised around a set of architectural views. Section 2 explains how the architecture is represented. Section 3 records the goals and constraints that shaped the design. Section 4 presents the use-case view, describing what the system does from the user's point of view. Section 5 presents the logical view (the main building blocks of the software), Section 6 the process view (how the system behaves while running), Section 7 the deployment view (where the software runs), and Section 8 the implementation view (how the code is organised). Section 9 describes how data is stored, Section 10 covers size and performance, and Section 11 explains how the architecture supports quality attributes such as reliability and security.

# **2\. Architectural Representation**

The architecture of AudioLIT is described using the well-known 4+1 view model, together with an additional data view. Each view looks at the system from a different angle and answers a different question, and each is expressed using standard UML diagrams supported by plain-language descriptions.

* Use-Case view \- what the system does, and how its parts work together to do it. This is described with a use-case diagram and scenario descriptions.

* Logical view \- the main software building blocks (packages and classes) and their responsibilities. This is described with class diagrams.

* Process view \- how the system behaves while it is running, especially how it handles several tasks at once. This is described with activity and sequence diagrams.

* Deployment view \- the physical setup: which programs run where. This is described with a deployment diagram.

* Implementation view \- how the source code is organised into layers and components. This is described with component diagrams.

* Data view \- how information is stored and for how long.

The use-case view sits at the centre: every element in the other views exists to support something a user wants to do. The following sections present each view in turn.

# **3\. Architectural Goals and Constraints**

## **3.1 Architectural Goals**

The design of AudioLIT is guided by a small number of clear goals:

* **Keep the interface responsive.** Running an AI model can take several seconds. The system must never freeze the web page while this happens; heavy work is carried out in the background and the user is kept informed of progress.

* **Make results reproducible.** The same input should always give the same explanation, so that a finding about bias or model behaviour can be checked and trusted by others.

* **Support many models.** A researcher should be able to bring their own speech model from Hugging Face and analyse it, for the supported model families, without changing the code.

* **Run on modest hardware.** The system must fit within the limited graphics-card memory of a free cloud GPU, and must still work (more slowly) on an ordinary computer with no GPU.

* **Preserve and extend ECHO 1.0.** Everything the original tool did must keep working; existing parts of the interface are extended rather than rewritten.

* **Be easy to extend.** Adding a new explanation method or a new kind of analysis should not require changes to the core of the system.

* **Be honest about its explanations.** When the system cannot produce a genuine explanation for a model, it must say so clearly rather than showing a made-up result.

## **3.2 Architectural Constraints**

Several constraints shape the design and limit the options available:

* **Full model access is required.** To explain a model, the system needs full internal access to it, so models are downloaded and run locally rather than accessed through a closed online service.

* **Limited GPU memory.** The set of models running at once must fit within roughly 3-5 GB of graphics memory so it works on a free cloud GPU, with an automatic fallback to the ordinary processor when no GPU is available.

* **Safe model files only.** Models downloaded from the internet are accepted only in a safe file format that cannot run hidden code when loaded.

* **No personal data is kept.** Uploaded audio is temporary and is not stored permanently; the system keeps only analysis records, never the audio itself.

* **Research-only datasets.** Some of the speech datasets used are for non-commercial research only, so the system is intended for academic use and displays the appropriate licence notices.

* **Building on an existing codebase.** AudioLIT extends the existing ECHO 1.0 code, so part of the work is reorganising and improving that code rather than writing everything new. Existing interface components are kept and extended.

* **Secure communication.** All communication between the browser and the server is encrypted, and passwords and secret keys are kept out of the source code.

A distinctive feature of AudioLIT, reflected throughout this document, is that it grows an existing academic tool into a more capable one rather than starting over. This shapes many of the decisions that follow: the design must fit alongside what already exists, reuse it where sensible, and add new capabilities cleanly. Being explicit about this boundary \- what is inherited, what is extended, and what is new \- is one of the main ways this document supports both the development team and the examiners.

## **3.3 Technology Choices**

AudioLIT keeps the main technologies used by ECHO 1.0 and updates them to current, stable versions. The user interface is built with React (a popular framework for building web interfaces) using TypeScript, and displays charts with Plotly. The backend server is built with FastAPI, a modern Python framework for building web services. Redis, a fast in-memory data store, is used both to cache results and to manage background work. A new database, MongoDB, is added to keep durable records of analyses and results.

The AI side uses PyTorch (a widely used machine-learning framework), models from Hugging Face such as Whisper (for transcription) and Wav2Vec2 (for emotion and deepfake analysis), and Captum, a library that produces the visual explanations. Audio is analysed using Librosa, a Python library for sound analysis. For reading and writing audio files the project uses the soundfile library, chosen because it is simple and well-supported. Background processing is handled by RQ (Redis Queue), a lightweight system for running slow tasks in the background without blocking the web server; RQ was chosen over heavier alternatives because it is simpler to set up and understand, which suits a small team. The versions of these libraries were chosen and tested together to make sure they work reliably as a set.

## **4.1 Use-Case Realizations**

The following describes how the system carries out six of the most important use cases. Each names the main software components involved, so that this section can be read together with the logical view in Section 5\. Sequence diagrams for these scenarios are given in Section 6\.

### **Use Case 1: Run a Multi-Task Analysis**

| Use case name | Run a Multi-Task Analysis (transcription, emotion, and deepfake detection) |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | ML Researcher |
| **Description** | The user uploads an audio clip and asks the system to transcribe it, detect its emotion, and check whether it is a deepfake \- all at once. This is the central scenario of the whole system. |
| **Preconditions** | A valid audio file (up to 100 MB and 15 minutes) has been selected, and suitable models are available. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The user uploads the clip and selects the analyses they want. 2\. The server checks the file, then checks whether this exact analysis has been done before and saved. 3\. If it has not, the server starts the work in the background and immediately gives the browser a way to follow the progress, so the page never freezes. 4\. Three background workers run the transcription, emotion, and deepfake analyses at the same time, each loading the model it needs. 5\. If an explanation such as an attention map cannot be produced genuinely, the system marks it as unavailable rather than showing a made-up result. 6\. The results are combined, saved for next time, and sent back to the browser, which displays the transcript, emotion chart, and deepfake score. |
| **Success post-condition** | The user sees the combined results, and the results are saved so an identical request later is instant. |
| **Fail post-condition** | If something fails, the user is shown a clear message and, where it makes sense, an option to try again. |
| **Extensions** | Because each analysis is saved separately, asking later for just one of them on the same clip returns instantly. |

### **Use Case 2: Retrieve a Saved Result**

| Use case name | Retrieve a Saved Result Instantly |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | ML Researcher |
| **Description** | The user submits a request that has already been analysed before. Instead of repeating the slow computation, the system returns the saved result immediately. This is what makes results reproducible and fast. |
| **Preconditions** | An identical analysis (same audio, model, and settings) has been done before and has not yet expired from the cache. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The server works out a unique fingerprint for the request based on the audio and the chosen settings. 2\. It looks up this fingerprint in the cache. 3\. If a matching result is found, it is returned straight away, without running any AI model. 4\. If the saved result is somehow damaged, it is discarded and the full analysis is run again. |
| **Success post-condition** | The user receives exactly the same result as before, in a fraction of a second. |
| **Fail post-condition** | A damaged saved result is simply recomputed; the system never returns a wrong answer from the cache. |
| **Extensions** | The cache only ever speeds things up; deleting it would never change any answer, only make the next request slower. |

### **Use Case 3: Generate an Explanation**

| Use case name | Generate a Visual Explanation of a Model's Decision |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | ML Researcher |
| **Description** | The user asks the system to show which parts of the audio most influenced a model's decision, using one of several explanation methods, and to display this as a heatmap over the sound. |
| **Preconditions** | A model is loaded and an analysis result exists or can be computed. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The user chooses an explanation method (such as Integrated Gradients, LIME, SHAP, or Grad-CAM) and a target. 2\. The request is sent to a background worker so it does not slow down other work. 3\. The chosen method calculates which parts of the audio mattered most for the decision. 4\. The result is turned into a coloured heatmap and drawn over the waveform and spectrogram. |
| **Success post-condition** | A clear, colour-coded explanation is shown over the audio and is saved for reuse. |
| **Fail post-condition** | If the explanation cannot be produced, the user is shown a helpful message. |
| **Extensions** | New explanation methods can be added later without changing the rest of the system. |

### **Use Case 4: Apply a Counterfactual Mutation**

| Use case name | Test a Model by Changing Part of the Audio |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | Software Engineer |
| **Description** | The user selects a region on the spectrogram and asks the system to alter it (for example, silence it or add noise), then compares what the model predicts before and after. This helps reveal what the model is really relying on. |
| **Preconditions** | A clip is loaded and shown on the spectrogram. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The user draws a box or lasso over a region of the spectrogram. 2\. The interface converts the drawn area into a precise time-and-frequency selection. 3\. The user can preview the change in the browser before sending it. 4\. A background worker applies the chosen change to a copy of the audio, always keeping the original untouched. 5\. The system re-runs the analysis on the changed audio and shows the difference side by side. |
| **Success post-condition** | The user sees a before-and-after comparison and a map of how the explanation changed. |
| **Fail post-condition** | An invalid selection returns a clear message and the original analysis is unaffected. |
| **Extensions** | Changes can be chained together for a step-by-step what-if exploration. |

### **Use Case 5: Add a Custom Model**

| Use case name | Add a Custom Model from Hugging Face |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | ML Researcher |
| **Description** | The user provides the name of a model from the Hugging Face hub. The system downloads it safely, prepares it for analysis, and makes it available alongside the built-in models. The same mechanism is used to load all of the system's own models. |
| **Preconditions** | A model name is provided and the model hub is reachable (or the model is already downloaded). |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The system checks whether the model is already available; if not, it downloads it. 2\. The model file is checked to make sure it is in the safe format before it is opened. 3\. The exact version is recorded so that results can always be reproduced later. 4\. For supported model families, the system prepares the model for analysis and lists the parts that can be explained. 5\. For an unsupported model, the system gives a clear message explaining that explanations are not available for it, rather than failing silently. |
| **Success post-condition** | A supported model is added and ready to analyse, alongside the built-in models. |
| **Fail post-condition** | An unsafe file, an unsupported model, or a download problem each produces a distinct, clear message. |
| **Extensions** | The system's own transcription and emotion models are loaded through this same mechanism, so there is one consistent way to manage all models. |

### **Use Case 6: Profile Bias and Check Explanation Quality**

| Use case name | Profile Accent Bias and Check Explanation Faithfulness |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor** | Trust-and-Safety Analyst |
| **Description** | The analyst runs a batch check across a speech dataset to measure how a model's accuracy differs across accents, and to check how faithful its explanations are. This is delivered at a focused, essential scope. |
| **Preconditions** | A suitable dataset is available and a model is selected. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The analyst starts the check; the system streams through the dataset rather than loading it all at once. 2\. For each accent group, the system measures the transcription error rate, reusing saved results so nothing is recomputed unnecessarily. 3\. To check explanation quality, the system hides the parts an explanation said were most important, re-runs the model, and measures how much the confidence drops. 4\. A ranked chart of accent differences and the explanation-quality score are produced and saved. |
| **Success post-condition** | A clear, ranked comparison across accents and an explanation-quality score are produced and stored for later reference. |
| **Fail post-condition** | A dataset or measurement error is reported clearly; incomplete results are not presented as if complete. |
| **Extensions** | More detailed fairness measures and additional explanation-quality checks are planned as future work. |

# **5\. Logical View**

## **5.1 Overview**

The software is organised into five main building blocks, arranged as a stack of layers. Each layer has one clear job and relies only on the layer below it. This keeps the design tidy and makes each part easier to build and test on its own. The five layers are:

* **Presentation layer** \- the web interface the user sees and interacts with, built with React. It extends the existing ECHO 1.0 interface with new panels.

* **Application layer (the gateway)** \- the FastAPI server that receives requests from the interface, checks them, and passes the heavy work on. It deliberately contains no AI code itself, so it always stays fast and responsive.

* **Orchestration layer** \- the background-processing system that shares the heavy work out among workers and collects the results.

* **Domain layer** \- the heart of the system: the code that loads models, runs the AI, produces explanations, and analyses audio. This is where most of the new work happens.

* **Infrastructure layer** \- the supporting services: the cache, the databases, and the tools for reading datasets and recording activity.

A key design rule is that the gateway never loads AI models directly. If it did, the web server would slow down every time a model ran. Instead, all heavy work is handed to the background layer, which is what keeps the interface responsive at all times. Another benefit of this layering is that the core AI logic can be tested on its own, without needing the web server or a graphics card.

![][image4]

**Figure 4\. The five layers of AudioLIT and how they depend on one another.**

**Diagram type:** *Layered structure diagram*

**Description:** Figure 4 shows the five layers as a stack. The interface is at the top, closest to the user, and the supporting services are at the bottom. Each layer uses only the one directly below it, so a change in one layer has a limited and predictable effect on the others. This simple rule is one of the most important decisions in the whole design, because it is what keeps a system with many moving parts understandable and maintainable.

## **5.2 Main Components**

Within these layers, the most important components are described below. Figure 5 shows them as a class diagram.

| Component | Responsibility |
| :---- | :---- |
| Model Registry | The single place through which every model is loaded \- both the built-in models and any custom model a user adds. It downloads models safely, records their exact version for reproducibility, and prepares them for explanation. |
| Explanation Strategies | A family of interchangeable explanation methods (Integrated Gradients, LIME, SHAP, Grad-CAM). New methods can be added as new members of this family without changing anything else. |
| Acoustic Profiler | Measures physical properties of the sound, such as its pitch and loudness over time, to show alongside the AI explanations. |
| Mutation Engine | Applies changes to a selected part of the audio (silencing, adding noise, shifting pitch, and so on) so the user can test how the model reacts, always keeping the original unchanged. |
| Bias Profiler and Faithfulness Auditor | Measure how a model's accuracy varies across accents, and how faithful its explanations are. |
| Cache Manager | Stores and retrieves previously computed results using a unique fingerprint of each request, so identical work is never repeated. |
| Task Orchestrator | Splits a multi-part request into separate background jobs, runs them together, and combines the results. |
| Workspace (interface state) | In the web interface, a single shared place that holds the current file, model, and results, which all the display panels read from so they always stay consistent. |

![][image5]

**Figure 5\. Class diagram showing the main components of AudioLIT and their relationships.**

**Diagram type:** *UML Class Diagram*

**Description:** Figure 5 shows the main components and how they connect. The Model Registry sits at the centre of the model-related components, because every model passes through it. The Explanation Strategies are shown as a family sharing a common interface, which is what allows them to be used interchangeably. The Cache Manager and Task Orchestrator are shown supporting the analysis flow, and the interface Workspace is shown as the single source of shared state that all display panels read from. The diagram deliberately shows the internal components rather than treating the system as a single block, so that responsibilities are clear and each part can be discussed on its own.

The Explanation Strategies component deserves special mention, because it is the key to keeping the system extensible. All explanation methods share the same simple interface, so the rest of the system does not need to know which one is being used. Adding a new method \- now or in the future \- means adding one new component, and nothing else changes. This is also how the more advanced research methods, if they are completed, can be slotted in without disturbing the committed system.

# **6\. Process View**

This section describes how AudioLIT behaves while it is running, and in particular how it handles slow AI tasks without making the user wait with a frozen screen. This is the most important dynamic aspect of the system.

## **6.1 How Work Is Shared Out**

When a user asks for an analysis, the web server does not do the heavy work itself. Instead, it places the work on a queue and hands it to a set of background workers, then immediately tells the browser how to follow the progress. This is managed by RQ, the background-task system, using Redis to hold the queue. There is one worker for each kind of model \- one for transcription, one for emotion, one for deepfake detection, and one for producing explanations \- plus a separate worker for the audio-editing tasks. Keeping a separate worker per model means each worker only ever needs to hold one model in memory, which is essential for staying within the limited graphics-card memory.

All the parts of the system communicate through Redis rather than talking to each other directly. This makes the system robust: if one part is restarted, the others carry on, and no work is lost because the jobs are safely held in the queue. When several analyses are requested together, they run at the same time on their separate workers, and the orchestrator waits for them all to finish and then combines the results. Combining the results of several parallel jobs is the trickiest part of this design, and is one of the first things the team will build and test carefully.

![][image6]

**Figure 6\. How AudioLIT shares heavy work among background workers.**

**Diagram type:** *Process/topology diagram*

**Description:** Figure 6 shows the running processes and how they exchange work through the shared store. The web server never runs a model itself; it only places jobs on the queue and passes progress back to the browser. Each worker is dedicated to one kind of model, which keeps each worker's memory use small and predictable. This arrangement is the direct result of the limited-memory constraint: rather than one large worker holding every model, several small workers each hold one.

## **6.2 A Typical Analysis, Step by Step**

Figure 7 is an activity diagram showing the flow of a typical multi-part analysis. The user uploads a clip and chooses the analyses. The server checks the file and then checks whether the result is already saved. If it is, the saved result is returned at once. If not, the work is placed on the queue, the workers run the analyses together, the results are combined and saved, and the finished result is sent back to the browser, which updates the display.

![][image7]

**Diagram type:** *UML Activity Diagram*

**Description:** Figure 7 shows the decision points and parallel work in a single analysis. The important branch is the check for a saved result: if one exists, the flow ends almost immediately with the saved answer; if not, the flow splits so that the separate analyses run at the same time, then joins again to combine them before saving and returning the result. The diagram highlights both the shortcut that makes repeated requests fast and the parallelism that makes a fresh multi-part analysis quick.

# **7\. Deployment View**

This section describes where the different parts of AudioLIT run. The system is packaged as a set of Docker containers \- self-contained bundles of software \- that run together on a single host computer. Docker makes the whole system easy to set up and ensures it runs the same way on a developer's machine, in a cloud environment, or on the demonstration computer. The target is an academic setting with a single host and a single group of users.

The containers are: the web interface, the gateway server, the background workers (for transcription, emotion, deepfake detection, explanations, and audio editing), the Redis store (used for both caching and the task queue), and the MongoDB database. When a graphics card is available, the model workers use it; when it is not, they automatically fall back to the ordinary processor, so the system still runs, just more slowly. Large model files are downloaded from the Hugging Face hub, and heavy work can optionally be sent to a free cloud GPU service when no local graphics card is present.

![][image9]

**Figure 9\. Deployment diagram showing where the parts of AudioLIT run.**

**Diagram type:** *UML Deployment Diagram*

**Description:** Figure 9 shows the physical arrangement. The user's browser is on the left, connecting over an encrypted internet connection to the application host. Inside the host, each box is a container running one part of the system, and the graphics card is shown attached to the model workers. On the right are the two external services the host connects to: the model hub, from which models are downloaded, and the optional cloud GPU service. Grouping the parts this way shows clearly which components share a machine, which share the graphics card, and which are external.

Because everything is defined in a single configuration file, the same setup runs on a laptop for development (without the graphics card) and on the demonstration host (with it). This is what makes it practical for a small team to develop and demonstrate the system from ordinary computers.

This section describes how the source code is organised. The code mirrors the five layers described in the logical view: presentation, application, orchestration, domain, and infrastructure. Each layer is only allowed to use the layer below it, which keeps the code tidy and prevents tangled dependencies. Figure 10 shows these layers as a component diagram.

Keeping the dependencies flowing in one direction like this is what prevents the code from becoming tangled and hard to change.

## **8.2 Building on the Existing ECHO 1.0 Code**

Because AudioLIT extends ECHO 1.0, an important part of the work is reorganising and improving the existing code rather than writing everything from scratch. The existing code is arranged more simply than AudioLIT's target structure, so parts of it are moved into the new layers. Each existing part is handled in one of four ways:

* **Reuse** \- kept as it is, because it already works and fits (for example, much of the existing interface).

* **Wrap** \- kept but given a cleaner interface so it fits the new structure (for example, the existing explanation code).

* **Refactor** \- the logic is kept but the structure is improved and untidy dependencies are removed (for example, the model-loading and dataset code).

* **Build new** \- written from scratch because ECHO 1.0 has no equivalent (for example, deepfake detection, the background-processing system, and the durable database).

This work is done in a careful order rather than all at once: the supporting services are set up first, then the model-loading is reorganised, then the explanation code is tidied, then the background-processing system replaces the simple queuing in the original code, and finally the new features are built on top. At each step the system is kept working and tested before moving on. This step-by-step approach reduces risk, which matters given the project's schedule.

# **9\. Data View**

AudioLIT stores information in two places, each with a clear and separate purpose. Importantly, neither of them ever stores the actual audio a user uploads \- only records about the analyses.

* **Redis** holds temporary, recomputable results \- the cache of previous analyses and the queue of background jobs. Everything in Redis can be recreated if lost, so it is kept only for a limited time to save space. This store was already used by ECHO 1.0 and is extended here.

* **MongoDB** is a new database added by AudioLIT. It keeps durable records that must survive over time: details of the models used, records of analyses, and the results of bias checks. These records are the lasting evidence of what was analysed and how.

The two are separated by how long the information needs to last. If something can be recreated on demand, it goes in Redis and is allowed to expire. If it is a record that must be kept \- so that a result can be reproduced or a bias finding can be referred back to \- it goes in MongoDB. A neat consequence of this design is that MongoDB stores only a reference to where a result is cached, not the result itself, so a small cache can support a large history of analyses. Records of bias checks are kept permanently, while ordinary analysis records expire after a day.

A specific design choice supports the goal of honest explanations: when the system cannot produce a genuine attention explanation, the record marks it as unavailable rather than storing a made-up one. This means the stored history itself can never misrepresent a fabricated explanation as real.

![][image12]

**Figure 12\. How AudioLIT stores information, and the separation between temporary and durable storage.**

**Diagram type:** *Data storage diagram*

**Description:** Figure 12 shows the two stores side by side. On one side, MongoDB holds the lasting records; on the other, Redis holds the temporary cache and the job queue. The arrow from the analysis records to the cache shows the space-saving idea at the heart of the design: the durable record does not contain the large result itself, only a pointer to where it is cached. The diagram also makes the privacy rule visible \- no box anywhere contains the uploaded audio.

# **10\. Size and Performance**

This section describes the performance the system aims for and the resources it needs. These are engineering targets, to be confirmed by testing. The single most important performance feature is the difference between a fresh analysis and a repeated one: a fresh multi-part analysis takes a few seconds, while a repeated request returns almost instantly from the cache. This large gap is exactly what the caching design is there to provide.

| Action | Target time |
| :---- | :---- |
| Return a previously saved result | Under a fifth of a second |
| Fresh transcription of a 15-second clip | A few seconds (on a graphics card) |
| Fresh multi-part analysis (transcription \+ emotion \+ deepfake) | Under about 8 seconds |
| Generate an explanation | Under about 8 seconds |
| Respond to a change drawn on the spectrogram | Half a second in the interface; a couple of seconds for the result |
| Accent bias check over a small batch | Under about 30 seconds, helped by reusing saved results |
| Download and prepare a new model | Under about a minute |

On memory, the set of models running at once is designed to fit within roughly 3-5 GB of graphics-card memory, comfortably inside the 16 GB available on a typical free cloud GPU, leaving room to spare. The cache is limited to a fixed size and automatically removes the least recently used results when it fills up. Large datasets are read a little at a time rather than loaded whole, so the system never needs an unreasonable amount of memory. When memory runs short or no graphics card is present, the system falls back to the ordinary processor rather than failing.

![][image13]

**Figure 13\. The performance targets and the memory budget.**

**Diagram type:** *Performance and resource chart*

**Description:** Figure 13 illustrates the two most important numbers in the design. The first is the very large gap between answering from the cache (almost instant) and running a fresh analysis (a few seconds); this gap is why caching is worth the effort. The second is the model memory use compared with the memory available on a free cloud graphics card, showing that the committed set of models fits comfortably with room to spare, which is what the memory constraint requires.

# **11\. Quality**

This section explains how the architecture supports the qualities expected of the system beyond its basic functions \- reliability, performance, maintainability, and security.

## **11.1 Reliability**

* If the graphics card is unavailable or runs out of memory, the system automatically switches to the ordinary processor rather than failing.

* If a background job fails for a temporary reason, it is retried a few times before giving up, and the user is told clearly whether trying again is worthwhile.

* If the connection to the model hub is down, the system reports a clear error quickly instead of hanging.

* A damaged cached result is detected and simply recomputed, so the cache can never cause a wrong answer.

* Because the parts of the system communicate only through the shared store, any part can be restarted without losing work, and an unfinished job can simply be resubmitted.

* Every unrecoverable failure is recorded, giving the team a clear record for debugging.

## **11.2 Performance and Maintainability**

Performance comes from four simple ideas: avoid repeating work by caching results, do several analyses at the same time, never make the user wait on a frozen screen, and keep memory use under control. Maintainability comes from the clean layering: the core AI logic has no dependence on the web framework, so it can be tested on its own, and new explanation methods or analyses can be added without disturbing the rest. All code passes automated tests and quality checks before it is accepted.

## **11.3 Security and Privacy**

Security is built in at the points where it matters most:

* Every uploaded file is checked for type, size, and validity before it is processed, to guard against harmful or oversized files.

* Models downloaded from the internet are accepted only in a safe format and are checked before being opened, so they cannot run hidden code.

* All communication between the browser and the server is encrypted, and secret keys are kept out of the source code.

* Uploaded audio is never stored permanently; the databases keep only analysis records, never the audio itself, and stored records contain no personal identifiers.

Because AudioLIT builds on existing code, the team also reviewed the security of the inherited parts and identified a few weaknesses to fix during development: a diagnostic feature that exposed too much information, an over-permissive setting on file access, and a weak check on access to datasets. These are being corrected as part of the project. Being open about inherited weaknesses and fixing them is important for a tool whose whole purpose is trustworthy analysis. Some features expected of a large commercial service, such as individual user accounts, are deliberately outside the scope of this academic project.

![][image14]

**Figure 14\. Where the main security checks are applied.**

**Diagram type:** *Security overview diagram*

**Description:** Figure 14 shows the points at which security is enforced. Most checks happen at the entry to the system, where uploads and downloaded models are validated before anything else is done with them \- the principle being to stop problems at the door rather than deeper inside. The diagram also shows the encrypted channel between the browser and the server, and the rule that the stored data contains no audio and no personal identifiers.

```mermaid
        Gateway["FastAPI Gateway"]
        SecVal["Security Validation\n• File Type Check\n• File Size Check\n• Audio Validation"]
        SafeModel["Safe Model Handling\n• safetensors Only\n• Model Verification\n• Version Recording"]
        Engine["Analysis Engine"]
        Storage[("Persistent Storage\nMongoDB / Redis")]
    end

    PrivacyRule["Privacy Rule:\nUploaded audio is NEVER stored"]
    StoredRecords["Stored Records:\nAnalysis Metadata, Bias Reports,\nNo Personal Identifiers"]

    Browser -->|HTTPS / TLS| Gateway
    Gateway --> SecVal
    Gateway -->|Secure Model Download| SafeModel
    HF --> SafeModel
    SecVal --> Engine
    SafeModel --> Engine
    Engine --> Storage
    Storage --> StoredRecords
    Engine -.-> PrivacyRule
```
